name: SWE-bench
creator: Princeton NLP & collaborators
tests: Fixing real bugs in real repositories, judged by unit tests.
summary: Gives a model a real GitHub issue from an open-source Python project and checks whether its code change makes the project's tests pass.

name: HumanEval
creator: OpenAI
tests: Writing a short correct function from a docstring.
summary: A classic set of hand-written Python function problems, each checked by running hidden tests. Useful as a baseline, though top models have largely mastered it.

name: LiveCodeBench
creator: LiveCodeBench team (academic)
tests: Code generation, self-repair and test prediction on fresh problems.
summary: Keeps collecting new contest problems over time, so you can test a model only on problems released after its training cutoff.

name: Aider leaderboards (Polyglot)
creator: Aider
tests: Practical multi-language code editing.
summary: Measures how well a model edits code in many programming languages inside the Aider coding assistant, including whether it follows the edit format.

name: BigCodeBench
creator: BigCode project
tests: Library-heavy, practical Python tasks.
summary: Programming tasks that require calling many real libraries correctly, closer to everyday developer work than puzzle-style problems.

name: GAIA
creator: Meta, Hugging Face & collaborators
tests: General assistant skills: browsing, file handling, multi-step reasoning.
summary: Questions that are easy for a person with a browser and tools but hard for AI assistants, each with one short, checkable answer.

name: τ-bench (tau-bench)
creator: Sierra Research
tests: Policy-following support agents with tools, plus consistency across repeated runs.
summary: Simulates a customer talking to an AI agent in domains like retail and airlines. The agent must follow company policy and use tools; the final database state is checked.

name: WebArena
creator: Carnegie Mellon University
tests: Autonomous web navigation and task completion.
summary: Self-hosted copies of realistic websites (shop, forum, code host and more) where an agent must complete tasks by clicking and typing.

name: OSWorld
creator: XLANG Lab & collaborators
tests: Computer-use agents operating real operating systems and apps.
summary: Puts an agent in a real computer environment and asks it to do tasks across desktop apps, checked by scripts.

name: Terminal-Bench
creator: Terminal-Bench team
tests: Agents working in the shell end to end.
summary: Tasks an agent must finish inside a sandboxed command-line terminal, such as compiling code, training models or setting up servers, checked by tests. It is now versioned continuously: 2.0 (89 tasks), 2.1 (the same 89 with 26–28 fixed), then 3.0 and 4.0 (4.0 recalibrated resources, removed 8 tasks and fixed 19).

name: BrowseComp
creator: OpenAI
tests: Deep, creative web research by browsing agents.
summary: 1,266 very hard-to-find facts with short answers that are easy to verify, built to test persistent web-browsing agents.

name: EQ-Bench Creative Writing
creator: EQ-Bench (Sam Paech)
tests: Creative writing quality judged against a rubric.
summary: Scores creative writing from models with an LLM judge using a detailed rubric, aiming to capture quality rather than just correctness.

name: AlpacaEval
creator: Stanford Tatsu Lab
tests: General helpfulness of chat responses.
summary: Compares a model's answers against a reference model's answers using an automatic LLM judge, with a correction for judges that prefer longer answers.

name: MT-Bench (LLM-as-a-judge paper)
creator: LMSYS
tests: Multi-turn conversation quality; how reliable LLM judges are.
summary: The paper that popularised using a strong model as a judge, with multi-turn questions and an analysis of where judges agree with humans and where they are biased.

name: IFEval
creator: Google
tests: Following explicit, verifiable instructions.
summary: Prompts with instructions a program can check automatically (word counts, formats, keywords), so no judge model is needed.

name: HarmBench
creator: Center for AI Safety & collaborators
tests: Robustness to jailbreaks and harmful requests.
summary: A standard framework for red-teaming: it tests how easily attacks can make a model produce harmful content and how well defences hold.

name: TruthfulQA
creator: Oxford & OpenAI researchers
tests: Truthfulness versus imitating human misconceptions.
summary: Questions designed so that common misconceptions are tempting; checks whether the model repeats popular falsehoods.

name: StrongREJECT
creator: UC Berkeley researchers
tests: Real effectiveness of jailbreak attacks.
summary: A better way to score jailbreaks: it checks whether the harmful answer is actually useful, not just whether the model refused.

name: SimpleQA
creator: OpenAI
tests: Short-form factuality and calibration.
summary: 4,326 short fact questions with one indisputable answer each; rewards models that answer correctly or admit they don't know instead of hallucinating.

name: XSTest
creator: Bocconi, Oxford & collaborators
tests: Over-refusal (exaggerated safety).
summary: Safe prompts that merely sound dangerous, to catch models that refuse too much.

name: HealthBench
creator: OpenAI
tests: Emergency referrals, handling uncertainty, global health, communication quality and more.
summary: 5,000 realistic, multi-turn health conversations, each graded against rubrics written by 262 physicians. Includes harder and consensus-validated subsets.

name: MedQA
creator: Jin et al.
tests: Medical exam knowledge.
summary: Multiple-choice questions from medical licensing exams. Easy to run, but exam-style and widely used, so it reveals little about real clinical conversations.

name: MedHELM
creator: Stanford CRFM
tests: Broad clinical tasks: documentation, decision support, patient communication and more.
summary: A holistic medical leaderboard covering many real clinical task types, not only exam questions.

name: KARMA-OpenMedEvalKit
creator: Eka Care
tests: Medical AI in Indian contexts, including speech recognition and record parsing.
summary: An open toolkit for evaluating medical AI with an emphasis on Indian healthcare, covering text, image and audio models and adding new India-focused datasets.

name: SAKHI
creator: SimPPL & collaborators
tests: Sensitive maternal-health answers in Indian languages.
summary: A maternal-health benchmark built around a WhatsApp chatbot for Hindi- and Marathi-speaking mothers, with rubric verdicts from Indian doctors to calibrate the LLM judge.

name: IndicGenBench
creator: Google Research
tests: Text generation quality in Indic languages.
summary: Generation tasks such as summarisation, translation and question answering across many Indian languages, including low-resource ones.

name: MILU
creator: AI4Bharat
tests: Multi-subject understanding in Indian languages and culture.
summary: A knowledge benchmark in Indian languages that includes India-specific subjects, not just translated Western exams.

name: Global-MMLU
creator: Cohere For AI & collaborators
tests: Knowledge across languages and cultural sensitivity.
summary: MMLU improved and translated into many languages, with labels marking which questions are culturally specific.

name: Samiksha
creator: Microsoft Research India & collaborators
tests: Culturally grounded health chatbot answers in Indian languages.
summary: A community-built pipeline for evaluating health chatbots in Hindi, Kannada and Malayalam, combining human raters with LLM judges.

name: Ragas
creator: Exploding Gradients
tests: Faithfulness, relevance and retrieval quality of your own RAG system.
summary: An open-source library of metrics for RAG apps and agents, such as whether an answer is faithful to the retrieved context.

name: BEIR
creator: UKP Lab & collaborators
tests: Zero-shot retrieval across diverse domains.
summary: A collection of retrieval datasets for testing how well search and embedding models work on domains they were not trained on.

name: MTEB Leaderboard
creator: MTEB community (Hugging Face Space)
tests: Embedding model quality for search and RAG.
summary: The public leaderboard of the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark, comparing embedding models on retrieval, classification, clustering, reranking and other tasks.

name: CRAG
creator: Meta & collaborators
tests: End-to-end RAG answer correctness and hallucination.
summary: A question-answering benchmark for RAG with mock web and knowledge-graph search, including questions whose answers change over time.

name: FRAMES
creator: Google
tests: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented answering.
summary: Questions that need facts from several documents combined, testing retrieval, reasoning and factuality together.

name: GPQA
creator: NYU & collaborators
tests: Expert-level science reasoning.
summary: Graduate-level science questions written by experts so that web search doesn't easily help.

name: Humanity's Last Exam
creator: Center for AI Safety & Scale AI
tests: Frontier academic knowledge and reasoning.
summary: Very hard questions contributed by experts across many fields, made to stay difficult after older benchmarks saturated.

name: Inspect Evals
creator: UK AI Security Institute & community
tests: Many benchmarks under one runner: coding, agents, safety, knowledge.
summary: A large, actively maintained collection of ready-to-run evals implemented in the Inspect framework.

name: OpenAI Evals
creator: OpenAI
tests: Building and running your own evals; community registry.
summary: A framework and open registry of evals, including templates for model-graded evaluation.

name: LLMJury rubric library
creator: LLMJury
tests: LLM-as-judge rubrics for support, RAG, summaries, code and tone.
summary: Paste-ready judge rubrics for questions like 'did the support reply resolve the request?', each with score meanings, examples and known failure modes. Made by a vendor.

name: Prompt Assay judge templates
creator: Prompt Assay
tests: Starter LLM-as-judge prompts.
summary: Copy-paste YAML judge templates covering basics like relevance and tone plus RAG, code, summarisation and agent traces. Made by a vendor.

name: SWE-bench-Live
creator: Microsoft Research & collaborators
tests: Fixing live software issues across languages and platforms, judged by tests in Docker.
summary: A continuously updated version of SWE-bench: real GitHub issues with Docker sandboxes, now covering multiple languages and operating systems, with new verified tasks added over time.

name: MLE-bench
creator: OpenAI
tests: End-to-end ML engineering: data prep, training, experimentation and submission quality.
summary: 75 real Kaggle machine-learning competitions where an agent must prepare data, train models and submit results, scored against human leaderboard medal thresholds.

name: Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL)
creator: UC Berkeley (Gorilla)
tests: Correct function/tool calling across simple, parallel, multi-turn and agentic tasks.
summary: Measures how accurately a model calls tools and functions, including parallel calls, multi-turn tool use and agentic scenarios, with an actively updated public leaderboard.

name: LiveBench
creator: LiveBench team (academic)
tests: Hard, contamination-limited tasks with verifiable ground-truth answers (no LLM judge).
summary: A regularly refreshed LLM benchmark with objective, auto-checkable answers across math, coding, reasoning and more, designed to limit training-data contamination.

name: Jev (TypeSafe AI)
creator: TypeSafe AI
tests: Not a benchmark: a tool for AI-judge / LLM-as-judge style scoring in your own evals.
summary: A commercial model API built for structured judgments rather than text: you send a state plus typed questions (pick a choice, score against a rubric, true/false likelihood) and get back typed answers with probabilities and confidence. Version 1.14.0 (announced 14 Oct 2026) adds experimental image inputs, a bounding-box answer type and longer context behind opt-in flags. Made by a vendor; paid API.

name: MMMU
creator: MMMU team (OSU, Waterloo & collaborators)
tests: Expert-level multimodal understanding and reasoning.
summary: About 11.5K college-level questions across six disciplines and 30 subjects, each pairing text with images such as charts, diagrams, maps and chemical structures.

name: MathVista
creator: UCLA, University of Washington & Microsoft Research
tests: Mathematical reasoning over figures, plots and images.
summary: 6,141 math problems set in visual contexts, drawn from 28 existing multimodal datasets plus three new ones (IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA).

name: MMBench
creator: OpenCompass (Shanghai AI Lab & collaborators)
tests: Broad perception and reasoning skills of vision-language models.
summary: A bilingual (English and Chinese) multiple-choice benchmark that breaks vision-language ability into fine-grained skills, and re-asks each question with the answer options shuffled, counting it correct only if the model is right every time.

name: ChartQA
creator: Masry et al. (academic)
tests: Question answering over charts.
summary: 9.6K human-written and 23.1K generated questions about real charts that need visual reading plus logical and arithmetic reasoning.

name: MMLU
creator: Hendrycks et al. (UC Berkeley & collaborators)
tests: World knowledge and problem solving across many school and professional subjects.
summary: Multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, from elementary mathematics and US history to computer science and law, testing broad academic and professional knowledge.

name: LMArena (Chatbot Arena)
creator: LMArena (started by LMSYS)
tests: Which models people prefer on their own real prompts, by pairwise human votes.
summary: A public site where people chat with two anonymous models side by side and vote for the better answer; the votes feed public leaderboards for text, coding, vision, image and video models.

name: HELM
creator: Stanford CRFM
tests: Standardised, multi-metric comparison of models across shared scenarios.
summary: Stanford's open framework and set of leaderboards for evaluating language models on many scenarios with several metrics at once, not just accuracy. Domain leaderboards include medicine (MedHELM), safety and vision-language models.

name: ARC-AGI-2
creator: ARC Prize
tests: Abstract reasoning and adapting to new problems from very few examples.
summary: Grid puzzles where the solver sees a few input-output examples, infers the hidden rule and must draw the exact output grid, with two tries per test input. The repo has 1,000 public training tasks and 120 public evaluation tasks; people in the creators' test sample averaged 66% on the evaluation set, and two private sets are kept back to limit leakage.

name: MMLU-Pro
creator: TIGER-AI-Lab
tests: Expert-level knowledge plus multi-step reasoning across subjects such as law, physics, health and economics.
summary: A harder follow-up to MMLU with over 12,000 exam and textbook questions in 14 subject areas and ten answer options instead of four. The authors report scores 16% to 33% lower than on MMLU and less sensitivity to prompt wording.

name: RULER
creator: NVIDIA
tests: How much of a long context window a model can really use.
summary: Generates synthetic long-context tests at whatever length you choose, with 13 tasks in 4 categories that go beyond finding a single needle in a haystack. Its results compare each model's advertised context length with the length at which it still performs well.

name: Arena-Hard-Auto
creator: LMArena
tests: Open-ended answers to hard user prompts, as a preview of how a model might fare on LMArena.
summary: An automatic benchmark built from hard prompts taken from Chatbot Arena, scored by LLM judges as a cheaper stand-in for human votes. Version 2.0 has 500 challenging real-world queries plus 250 creative writing prompts.

name: AgentDojo
creator: ETH Zurich (SPY Lab) & Invariant Labs
tests: Agent task success and robustness to prompt injection attacks.
summary: An extensible environment for testing whether tool-using agents can be hijacked by prompt injections hidden in the data their tools return. The paper's release has 97 realistic tasks, such as handling email, e-banking and travel bookings, and 629 security test cases, with pluggable attacks and defences.

name: SWE-Bench Pro
creator: Scale AI
tests: Coding agents implementing larger, well-specified changes in real codebases.
summary: Long, multi-file software tasks from 41 maintained repositories (Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go). An agent must produce a patch that passes human-reviewed tests. Public set of 731 tasks (v1) or 642 re-validated tasks (V2); commercial and held-out sets stay private.

name: DeepEval
creator: Confident AI
tests: Your own LLM app, RAG pipeline or agent, as pass/fail tests in CI.
summary: An open-source Python framework for unit-testing LLM apps like pytest, with LLM-judged metrics for RAG (faithfulness, answer relevancy, contextual precision and recall), agents (task completion, tool correctness) and custom criteria (G-Eval).

name: ARC-AGI-3
creator: ARC Prize Foundation
tests: Exploration, goal inference, world-modelling and planning in new environments.
summary: Interactive, turn-based game environments with no instructions: an agent must explore, work out the goal and the rules, and finish each level in as few actions as a first-time human. 25 public demo environments, 55 semi-private and 55 fully private; scored by action efficiency against human baselines (RHAE).

name: Promptfoo
creator: Promptfoo (now part of OpenAI)
tests: Your own prompts, models and LLM apps, with deterministic and LLM-graded assertions.
summary: An open-source (MIT) command-line tool for testing prompts, agents and RAG apps from declarative YAML configs, comparing models side by side, running checks in CI, and red-teaming LLM apps for vulnerabilities.

name: Agent-as-a-Judge (DevAI)
creator: Meta AI & KAUST
tests: Coding agents on full AI-development tasks, judged step by step instead of pass/fail.
summary: A method that uses an agent, which can read files, locate code and inspect trajectories, to judge other agents requirement by requirement, plus DevAI: 55 AI-development tasks with 365 hierarchical requirements. In the paper it agreed with human consensus about 90% of the time versus about 70% for LLM-as-a-judge.

name: lm-evaluation-harness
creator: EleutherAI
tests: Models on standard academic benchmarks with consistent prompts.
summary: An open-source framework for running over 60 standard academic benchmarks, with hundreds of subtasks and variants, against language models. It powered Hugging Face's Open LLM Leaderboard.

name: MATH
creator: Hendrycks et al. (UC Berkeley)
tests: Multi-step maths reasoning with exact answers.
summary: 12,500 competition mathematics problems with full step-by-step solutions (NeurIPS 2021). Many reports use the 500-problem MATH-500 subset.

name: GSM8K
creator: OpenAI
tests: Basic multi-step arithmetic reasoning.
summary: 8.5K grade-school maths word problems written by people: 7.5K for training and 1K for testing. Frontier models now score near the ceiling.

name: EvalPlus (HumanEval+ / MBPP+)
creator: EvalPlus team
tests: Function-level code generation with thorough tests.
summary: Stricter versions of HumanEval and MBPP: HumanEval+ has 80x more tests and MBPP+ 35x more, catching code that passed only the original thin tests.

name: SWE-Lancer
creator: OpenAI
tests: Coding agents on paid, real-world freelance work.
summary: Over 1,400 real Upwork freelance software tasks worth $1 million in payouts, from $50 bug fixes to $32,000 features, graded by end-to-end tests, plus managerial proposal-choice tasks.

name: SciCode
creator: SciCode team
tests: Writing code for real scientific research problems.
summary: 80 research-level scientific coding problems split into 338 subproblems across the natural sciences and maths. Part of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index.

name: Cybench
creator: Stanford (Cybench team)
tests: Agents on offensive cybersecurity tasks.
summary: 40 professional Capture the Flag tasks from four CTF competitions, with subtasks for partial credit, for measuring AI agents' cybersecurity capabilities and risks.

name: Langfuse
creator: Langfuse
tests: Your own LLM app, on production traces and test datasets.
summary: An open-source, self-hostable platform for tracing LLM apps and agents and scoring them with LLM-as-a-judge evaluators, datasets and experiments.

name: τ²-bench / τ³-bench (tau2-bench)
creator: Sierra Research
tests: Support agents that follow policy, use tools and coach a user who also takes actions.
summary: The successor to τ-bench. Its telecom domain lets both the agent and the simulated user act with tools on a shared system, so the agent has to guide the user through fixes. The current τ³ release adds a banking knowledge-retrieval domain and full-duplex voice tests.

name: MMMU-Pro
creator: MMMU team (OSU, Waterloo & collaborators)
tests: Multimodal reasoning when the model must read the question from the image itself.
summary: A harder rebuild of MMMU: questions a text-only model could answer were removed, more answer options were added, and a vision-only setting puts the whole question inside an image. In the paper, models scored 16.8% to 26.9%, far below their MMMU results.

name: Arize Phoenix
creator: Arize AI
tests: Your own LLM app or agent, on traces and test datasets.
summary: A self-hostable tool for tracing and evaluating LLM apps: OpenTelemetry-based traces, LLM-graded evals for answers and retrieval, versioned datasets and experiments. It is released under the Elastic License 2.0; Arize sells a separate managed product (Arize AX).

name: DROP
creator: Dua et al. (AllenNLP & collaborators)
tests: Reading comprehension that needs arithmetic and counting over the text.
summary: 96K crowdsourced, adversarially written reading questions where the model must locate several facts in a paragraph and then add, count or sort them. At release the best system reached 32.7% F1 against 96.0% for expert humans.

name: OpenAI simple-evals
creator: OpenAI
tests: Chat models on standard benchmarks with simple zero-shot prompts.
summary: OpenAI's small library for running MMLU, MATH, GPQA, DROP, MGSM, HumanEval, SimpleQA, BrowseComp and HealthBench with zero-shot, chain-of-thought prompts, released to show how its published numbers were produced. Since July 2025 it gets no new models or results but keeps the reference code for HealthBench, BrowseComp and SimpleQA.

name: FACTS Grounding
creator: Google DeepMind & Google Research
tests: Whether long answers stay grounded in a supplied document.
summary: Each prompt pairs a user request with a document of up to 32K tokens; the long answer must meet the request and be fully supported by the document. Several judge models score it, and the Kaggle leaderboard keeps a private split next to 860 public examples.

name: RE-Bench
creator: METR
tests: Agents on AI research and engineering work, compared with human experts.
summary: 7 open-ended ML research-engineering environments, with data from 71 eight-hour attempts by 61 human experts. With 2 hours per environment the best agents scored 4x higher than the experts, but people gained more from extra time and reached 2x the top agent's score at 32 hours.

name: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)
creator: Suzgun et al. (from Google's BIG-Bench)
tests: Multi-step reasoning across varied puzzle-style tasks.
summary: 23 BIG-Bench tasks on which earlier language models did worse than the average human rater. The paper showed chain-of-thought prompting let Codex pass the human average on 17 of the 23, so scores depend heavily on the prompting method.

name: AppWorld
creator: Stony Brook University NLP & collaborators
tests: Coding agents that operate several apps through APIs to finish daily tasks.
summary: A simulated world of 9 everyday apps with 457 APIs, used by about 100 fictional people, plus 750 tasks an agent solves by writing code against those APIs. State-based tests accept different valid solutions and also catch collateral damage to other data.

name: Taste-Bench
creator: City University of Hong Kong & Microsoft
tests: An agent's judgement at long-horizon decision points, not just end-to-end task success.
summary: 502 two-option questions cut from real agent runs: the model sees the task and the run up to a decision point, then picks which next step the rest of the run proved better. Forks come from software-engineering runs on SWE-bench and SWE-bench Pro and from ML-research runs in METR's MALT transcripts; the paper reports the best model at 59.7%.

name: Mind2Web
creator: The Ohio State University
tests: Generalist web agents completing multi-step tasks across unseen sites and domains.
summary: 2,350 tasks written for 137 real websites across 31 domains, such as booking flights or finding receipts, used to check whether a web agent can follow a plain-language instruction on sites it has not seen before.

name: Spider 2.0
creator: XLANG Lab
tests: Writing and running SQL in realistic enterprise data workflows.
summary: 632 text-to-SQL workflow problems taken from enterprise database use, often on databases with over 1,000 columns in systems like BigQuery and Snowflake. Answers frequently need several long SQL queries, far beyond classic single-query text-to-SQL sets.

name: LongBench v2
creator: LongBench team (THUDM, Tsinghua)
tests: Deep understanding and reasoning over very long inputs.
summary: 503 hard multiple-choice questions over contexts from 8k to 2M words, covering single- and multi-document QA, long in-context learning, long dialogue history, code repositories and structured data. The format keeps scoring simple and reliable.

name: WMDP
creator: Center for AI Safety & collaborators
tests: Hazardous dual-use knowledge and how well unlearning removes it.
summary: 3,668 multiple-choice questions that act as a stand-in for hazardous knowledge in biosecurity, cybersecurity and chemical security. It is used both to measure how much risky knowledge a model holds and to test unlearning methods that try to remove it.

name: MedMCQA
creator: Pal, Umapathi & Sankarasubbu
tests: Medical entrance-exam knowledge across many subjects.
summary: More than 194k multiple-choice questions from India's AIIMS and NEET PG medical entrance exams, spanning 21 subjects and about 2.4k topics, with explanations. Good for broad medical knowledge checks, though exam questions say little about real patient conversations.

name: ExtractBench (LlamaIndex)
creator: LlamaIndex
tests: Document-extraction systems, VLMs and coding agents filling a schema from long business documents.
summary: Schema-guided extraction from enterprise documents: given a full document and a JSON schema, a system must return every requested value with evidence. 370 documents, 4,869 pages, 67 document types and 8 business domains, scored without an LLM judge on value F1, record completeness, word- and page-level grounding and measured cost. Built by LlamaIndex, which also sells extraction tools that appear on its leaderboard.

name: ExtractBench Pro (LlamaIndex)
creator: LlamaIndex
tests: Extraction systems on long-tail documents with charts, diagrams and house rules.
summary: The harder companion to ExtractBench, released October 2026: 100 synthetic documents (2,622 pages, 86 document types, 144,141 expected values) where many values cannot be copied from the page. They must be read off charts or drawings, counted under the document's own rules, or decoded with its own jargon. Same evaluator as ExtractBench; the headline metric is the share of documents extracted perfectly.

name: ParseBench (LlamaIndex)
creator: LlamaIndex
tests: Document parsers and VLMs turning PDFs into structured output agents can act on.
summary: About 2,000 human-verified pages from insurance, finance and government documents, used to check whether PDF parsers keep what an agent needs: table structure, chart data, faithful content, meaningful formatting such as strikethrough, and visual grounding. Scoring is deterministic and rule-based by default. Built by LlamaIndex, whose LlamaParse is on its leaderboard.

name: HELMET
creator: Princeton NLP
tests: Long-context models on recall, RAG, re-ranking, citation, long-document QA, summarisation and in-context learning.
summary: A long-context benchmark with seven application-style categories, controllable input lengths up to 128K tokens, model-based scoring and few-shot prompts so base models can be tested too. Its study of 59 models found that needle-in-a-haystack scores do not reliably predict real long-context performance.

name: FinanceBench
creator: Patronus AI
tests: RAG and long-context systems answering questions from financial reports.
summary: Open-book questions about public companies' financial filings, with human-written answers and evidence strings. The full set has 10,231 questions; 150 annotated examples are open source. In the paper, GPT-4-Turbo with retrieval answered wrongly or refused on 81% of the sampled questions.

name: AgentBench
creator: Tsinghua University (THUDM) & collaborators
tests: Multi-turn agent reasoning and decision-making across varied environments.
summary: Tests an LLM acting as an agent across eight interactive environments in the original paper, such as an operating system shell, databases, a knowledge graph and web shopping. The current repo is a function-calling version that runs five of these tasks in Docker; older releases stay available as v0.1 and v0.2.

name: VisualWebArena
creator: Carnegie Mellon University
tests: Multimodal web agents on visually grounded browsing tasks.
summary: A visual follow-up to WebArena: 910 web tasks on self-hosted classifieds, shopping and forum sites where the agent has to understand images and page layout, not just text. Success is checked by executing against the site state.

name: TheAgentCompany
creator: Carnegie Mellon University & collaborators
tests: Agents doing realistic, multi-step workplace tasks end to end.
summary: A simulated small software company with its own GitLab, Plane, ownCloud and RocketChat, where agents do work tasks by browsing, coding, running programs and messaging simulated coworkers. In the paper, the strongest baseline agent finished 30% of tasks on its own.

name: CRUXEval
creator: Meta AI (FAIR) & collaborators
tests: Code reasoning and mental execution.
summary: 800 short Python functions, each with an input-output pair. The model either predicts the output from the input (CRUXEval-O) or finds an input that yields the output (CRUXEval-I), so it measures reading and executing code rather than writing it.

name: Multi-SWE-bench
creator: ByteDance Seed
tests: Coding agents fixing real issues in non-Python repositories.
summary: SWE-bench-style issue resolving beyond Python: 1,632 instances across Java, TypeScript, JavaScript, Go, Rust, C and C++, filtered from 2,456 candidates by 68 expert annotators. Smaller mini (400) and flash (300) sets exist for cheaper runs. Accepted to the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks track.

name: SWE-PolyBench
creator: Amazon Science
tests: Coding agents across four languages at repository scale.
summary: Repository-level coding tasks from 2,110 curated issues in Java, JavaScript, TypeScript and Python, with a 500-issue stratified subset and a 382-issue Verified split released in August 2025. Besides pass rate it reports file and code-node retrieval metrics.

name: RewardBench
creator: Allen Institute for AI (Ai2)
tests: Reward models and LLM-as-judge models picking the correct response.
summary: A benchmark and toolkit for evaluating reward models, including DPO-style models and LLM judges. RewardBench 2 has 1,865 prompts across six domains (factuality, precise instruction following, math, safety, focus and ties), mostly unseen human prompts, scored best-of-4 so random guessing gets 25%. Its paper reports that models score about 20 points lower than on the original RewardBench.

name: MathArena
creator: ETH Zurich SRI Lab and INSAIT
tests: Competition math reasoning and natural-language proof writing.
summary: Evaluates LLMs on math competitions soon after the problems are released, such as AIME, HMMT, USAMO and IMO, to limit training-data contamination. Final answers are checked by a rule-based parser with manual review, and proof problems are graded by two human judges. Its paper reports strong signs of contamination in AIME 2024.

name: WildBench
creator: Allen Institute for AI (Ai2)
tests: Chat assistants on hard, real-world user requests across 12 task types.
summary: 1,024 challenging tasks picked from real user conversations in the WildChat logs, judged automatically by an LLM using a checklist for each task. It reports WB-Score for single responses and WB-Reward for pairwise comparisons against three baseline models, with an optional length penalty to reduce bias toward longer answers.

name: NoLiMa
creator: Adobe Research
tests: Long-context retrieval that needs inference, not literal matching.
summary: A needle-in-a-haystack style long-context test where the question and the hidden fact share very few words, so a model has to make a latent association instead of matching text. The ICML 2025 paper found that 10 of 12 models tested fell below half of their short-context score by 32K tokens.
